reference.source: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases / CDC guidance
clinicalPearls: A mosquito-borne alphavirus of eastern North America maintained in a bird reservoir with Culiseta mosquitoes, spilling over to humans and horses via bridge-vector mosquitoes near freshwater swamps

Most infections are asymptomatic or febrile, but eastern equine encephalitis produces the most severe of the arboviral encephalitides in North America with very high mortality among those with neuroinvasive disease
Neuroinvasive illness presents with high fever, headache, vomiting, seizures, and rapidly progressive obtundation, often after a brief prodrome
Young children and older adults are at greatest risk of severe disease and neurological sequelae
Magnetic resonance imaging characteristically shows lesions in the basal ganglia and thalami, which can help differentiate it from other encephalitides
There is no specific antiviral or licensed human vaccine; management is intensive supportive and neuroprotective care with seizure and intracranial pressure control
Diagnosis rests on cerebrospinal fluid and serum serology (IgM) and, where available, molecular testing, alongside a summer mosquito-exposure history
reference.pathophysiology: Eastern equine encephalitis virus cycles between passerine birds and ornithophilic mosquitoes in freshwater swamp habitats, with bridge-vector mosquitoes transmitting to incidental hosts such as humans and horses that do not sustain transmission. After a bite, viral replication and viraemia can be followed by neuroinvasion across the blood-brain barrier. In the central nervous system the virus causes widespread neuronal infection, intense inflammation, and vasculitis, with a predilection for deep grey-matter structures, producing severe oedema and neuronal destruction that underlie the high fatality and neurological sequelae.
additionalDifferentials: Other arboviral encephalitides such as St Louis or La Crosse encephalitis
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid IgM serology for eastern equine encephalitis virus
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis typically showing pleocytosis and raised protein
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain looking for basal ganglia and thalamic involvement
Molecular testing (RT-PCR) on cerebrospinal fluid where available, recognising limited sensitivity late in disease
Electroencephalography to characterise seizure activity and encephalopathy
Testing to exclude treatable causes, particularly herpes simplex virus
redFlags: Focal neurological deficits with basal ganglia or thalamic lesions on imaging
Extremes of age with neuroinvasive disease
reference.prognosis: Neuroinvasive eastern equine encephalitis carries one of the highest case-fatality rates of the arboviral encephalitides, and many survivors are left with significant long-term neurological disability.
pitfalls: Delaying empirical aciclovir for possible herpes simplex encephalitis while awaiting arboviral results
Relying on molecular testing alone, since RT-PCR sensitivity in cerebrospinal fluid is limited and serology is often required
Underestimating rapid deterioration and delaying intensive care admission
Overlooking the summer mosquito-exposure history in swampy endemic regions
Failing to recognise characteristic deep grey-matter imaging findings
